newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Feb housing starts rebound sharply on weather.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Feb housing starts rebound sharply on weather.

text.p: U.S. housing starts surprised financial markets with a more robust than expected February figure, hinting that weather-related factors and economic fundamentals are providing an offsetting stimulus to the housing sector, analysts said.

"(The housing report) shows some of the rebound in February's mild weather after some weather-related problems depressed the January and December numbers," said Michael Strauss, chief economist at Sanwa Securities (USA) Co.
The Commerce Department said housing starts jumped 12.2 percent, to 1.528 million units on an annualized basis in February, the highest level since 1.564 million units in March 1994.
Wall Street economists had forecast February starts at a 1.45 million unit annual rate. The January figure was revised upward to 1.362 million units.
Analysts said the structural surge in housing activity amid rising mortgage rates is a sign that other factors are providing a stimulus to the housing sector.

"This doesn't come as any surprise," said Kevin Flanagan, economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. "You've got higher income growth, good job opportunities, soaring confidence levels...all the ingredients that should support housing for the near future," he said.

Although sound economic fundamentals and benign weather in the Northeast and upper Midwest influenced the robust starts number in February, a few analysts said housing permits data is probably a better yardstick.

"The permits data is probably more realistic than the starts numbers," said Marilyn Schaja, money market economist, at DLJ Securities Corp. "So, there will probably be some reversal in the future months," she said.
Permits for new housing construction increased 3.0 percent in February, up from an upwardly revised -1.5 percent in January.
Regionally, February permits in the Northeast rose 8.8 percent but starts dropped 26.9 percent, the biggest decline for the region since a 37.8-percent decrease in December 1990.
Yet starts in the Midwest jumped 51.6 percent and permits rose 5.0 percent.

Economists said that while housing starts are unlikely to lead the Fed to change its interest rate policy, the robust housing report is more fodder backing the notion that Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan might proceed with a pre-emptive short-term interest rate hike at next Tuesday's policy setting meeting.
"It adds some reasons for why the Fed is probably going to need to raise rates next week," Sanwa's Strauss added.
